name: Auckland
tagline: City of sails between two harbours and green volcanoes.
whenBlurb: February to March and November to December give warm, settled harbour days, the crimson pōhutukawa bloom and the sailing calendar; skip the wet, cool June-August winter that belongs indoors.

ourTake.lede: Auckland is a jumping-off point as much as a destination, and its best hours are spent on or across the water. Give the museum and the Sky Tower a morning, then get out to Waiheke's vineyards or the black-sand west coast, which is where the region actually earns its reputation. The mistake is treating it as a city break; treat it as a base for the Hauraki Gulf and the wine islands instead.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a gentle, green gateway to New Zealand with harbour sailing, island vineyards and easy day-trips.
ourTake.skipIf: You are chasing the dramatic alpine scenery and adrenaline that live on the South Island, not the North.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Park Hyatt Auckland
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller Readers' Choice Awards 2023, Top hotels in Australia & New Zealand
Park Hyatt, Hyatt's maison flagship tier
items.description: The country's most polished five-star house, a low, calm waterfront landmark on the Viaduct edge, with a 25-metre pool and the acclaimed Onemata dining room.

items.name: Cordis, Auckland
credentials: Langham Hospitality Group, Cordis luxury collection
Forbes Travel Guide Recommended, a landmark Auckland five-star
items.description: A large, gracious five-star hotel by Langham Hospitality Group, a heated rooftop infinity pool, a serious spa and the celebrated Chef's dining.

items.name: The Grand by SkyCity
credentials: Home to Metita, Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025 Hotel Restaurant of the Year
A landmark five-star hotel of the City Centre
items.description: A grand five-star tower in the SkyCity precinct, home to Metita, the country's Hotel Restaurant of the Year, with a lap pool and spa.

items.name: Sofitel Auckland Viaduct Harbour
credentials: Sofitel, Accor's French luxury maison brand
A landmark Viaduct Harbour five-star hotel
items.description: A French-accented five-star on the marina's edge, waterfront suites, a heated pool and a graceful spa on the Viaduct.

items.name: The Hotel Britomart
credentials: World's first 5 Green Star-rated hotel (New Zealand Green Building Council)
Condé Nast Traveller Hot List, the only New Zealand hotel listed
items.description: New Zealand's first 5 Green Star hotel, a warm, timber-lined design house in the heart of the Britomart dining and shopping precinct.

items.name: SO/ Auckland
credentials: SO/ by Accor, the group's design-led luxury maison brand
Formerly The Grand by SkyCity heritage building, a landmark City Centre address
items.description: Accor's fashion-led SO/ maison brand in a heritage tower, bold design, a rooftop bar and harbour views over the city edge.

items.name: QT Auckland
credentials: QT Hotels, a landmark design hotel brand
A landmark Viaduct Harbour design hotel
items.description: A playful, art-filled design hotel on the Viaduct waterfront, colour, character and one of the city's liveliest rooftop bars.

items.name: Hotel DeBrett
credentials: A landmark heritage boutique hotel (1925 Art Deco building)
Condé Nast Traveller, recognised Auckland boutique stay
items.description: A beloved boutique hotel in a restored 1925 Art Deco building, individually designed rooms and a buzzing courtyard bar in the heart of the city.

items.name: Sky Tower
credentials: Tripadvisor Travellers' Choice, #1 Auckland attraction
items.description: Auckland's 328-metre spire and the tallest structure in the Southern Hemisphere, with three observation decks and glass floor panels that drop the eye straight to the street 186 metres below. On a clear day the view runs 80 kilometres over the Waitematā, the Hauraki Gulf islands and the ring of volcanic cones; take the family up at dusk for the city lighting up, then dine at the revolving Orbit 360 one floor down.

items.name: SkyWalk & SkyJump at the Sky Tower
items.description: For the thrill-seeker in the family: a harnessed walk on a 1.2-metre ledge around the tower's rim at 192 metres with no handrails, or a wire-guided base-jump-style plunge at up to 85 km/h. Grandparents can watch in comfort from the observation deck while the teenagers step off the edge; both run on private timed slots.

items.name: Auckland War Memorial Museum (Tāmaki Paenga Hira)
items.description: A neoclassical temple crowning the Domain, holding the world's finest collection of Māori and Pacific treasures alongside a carved meeting house and a full-sized war canoe. Book the twice-daily Māori cultural performance of song, haka and story for a dignified, multi-generational introduction to the culture of the land, then take tea on the terrace over the harbour.

items.name: Auckland Art Gallery Toi o Tāmaki
credentials: World Building of the Year 2013 (World Architecture Festival)
items.description: New Zealand's oldest and largest art institution, with a soaring kauri-canopy roof over 17,000 works spanning European masters, contemporary New Zealand painting and a moving room of Māori ancestral portraits by Goldie and Lindauer. Entry to the permanent collection is free and it sits at the edge of Albert Park, an easy, cultured hour for any age.

items.name: Viaduct Harbour
items.description: The former America's Cup basin, now a ring of superyachts, waterside restaurants and champagne bars where Auckland comes to be seen. It is the natural place to base an evening on the water and the departure point for private charters and the America's Cup sailing yachts.

items.name: Wynyard Quarter & Silo Park
items.description: A reclaimed industrial waterfront turned promenade of playgrounds, seafood restaurants and the landmark red Silo Park, with summer outdoor cinema and night markets among the old cement silos. A relaxed, stroller-friendly stretch to walk off dinner as the harbour lights come on.

items.name: America's Cup Sailing on the Waitematā
items.description: Take the helm or simply recline on the rail of a genuine former America's Cup grand-prix racing yacht as it heels across the harbour past the Harbour Bridge and skyline. No experience needed and the whole family can crew or watch; private full-boat charters make it a discreet, unforgettable two hours on the City of Sails.

items.name: Auckland Harbour Bridge Climb
items.description: A guided harnessed walk up the arch of the 1959 road bridge to the summit at 65 metres, with the Waitematā, the yachts and Rangitoto laid out beneath you. There is also a bungy off a purpose-built pod for the daring; the climb itself is a gentle, steady ascent suitable for confident older children and grandparents alike.

items.name: Mission Bay & Tamaki Drive
items.description: Auckland's most beloved seaside promenade, a golden crescent of beach with an Art Deco fountain, gelato and waterfront cafés looking straight across to Rangitoto. Drive or cycle the full sweep of Tamaki Drive past the yacht basins for the classic City of Sails afternoon; easy and safe for all ages.

items.name: Bastion Point & the Michael Joseph Savage Memorial
items.description: A clifftop of consecrated ground above Tamaki Drive, its Art Deco obelisk and formal gardens giving a sweeping panorama over the harbour to Rangitoto. It is also one of the most significant sites in modern Māori history, scene of the 506-day 1977–78 land occupation; a quiet, contemplative stop with a story worth a guide.

items.name: Maungawhau / Mount Eden
items.description: Auckland's highest volcanic cone at 196 metres, with a perfect grassy crater at the top and a full 360-degree sweep of the isthmus and both harbours. Walking to the summit is protected as an ancestral maunga, but the reward is the definitive view of the volcanic city; keep to the paths as the crater is sacred.

items.name: Maungakiekie / One Tree Hill & Cornwall Park
items.description: A 182-metre cone crowned by an obelisk and ringed by the largest pre-European earthwork fortifications on earth, set in the gifted parkland of Cornwall Park with grazing sheep and centenarian oaks. A gentle drive or walk to the summit and a picnic under the trees make an idyllic, unhurried family morning.

items.name: Auckland Domain & the Wintergardens
items.description: The city's oldest park, spread over an ancient volcano, with the Wintergardens' twin Edwardian glasshouses of tropical and cool-climate blooms and a fern-filled sunken quarry. A serene, shaded stroll that pairs naturally with the Museum on the same hill.

items.name: Karangahape Road (K' Road)
credentials: Time Out, World's Coolest Streets 2022
items.description: Auckland's most characterful strip, a mile of vintage stores, galleries, tiny wine bars and cuisines from Malaysian to modern Brazilian, named among the world's coolest streets by Time Out. Go for the atmosphere and the food rather than luxury shopping; it is bohemian, alive and refreshingly unpolished.

items.name: Ponsonby Road
items.description: Nicknamed 'the dining room of Auckland', a village high street of Victorian villas turned into the city's densest run of good restaurants, cafés and design boutiques, anchored by the food-hall energy of Ponsonby Central. The place to spend a leisurely lunch and afternoon; several kitchens handle vegetarian and Indian palates well.

items.name: Britomart Precinct
items.description: The sleekest quarter of the central city, a cluster of restored heritage warehouses now holding New Zealand designer boutiques, top restaurants and the design-led Hotel Britomart, steps from the ferry terminal. The natural base for a stylish, walkable stay and a Saturday morning market.

items.name: SEA LIFE Kelly Tarlton's Aquarium
items.description: Built into old harbourside sewage tanks by a New Zealand diving pioneer, with curved underwater tunnels of sharks and stingrays and an Antarctic ice enclosure of penguins. A reliable, weather-proof couple of hours that delights younger children on Tamaki Drive.

items.name: New Zealand Maritime Museum (Hui Te Ananui a Tangaroa)
items.description: On Hobson Wharf beside the Viaduct, tracing the ocean story from the first Polynesian voyagers to America's Cup glory, with heritage vessels moored outside that still sail the harbour. A short guided sail on a classic scow or steamer is the highlight for a maritime-minded family.

items.name: Waiheke Island, vineyards, beaches & Oneroa
items.description: A 40-minute ferry to a warmer, sunnier island of forty white-sand beaches and world-class vineyards, where cellar doors like Mudbrick, Cable Bay and Stonyridge serve Bordeaux-style reds over Hauraki Gulf views back to the skyline. The essential Auckland day trip; a private driver-guide or helicopter transfer lets multi-generational groups linger over long lunches without watching the clock.

items.name: Mudbrick Vineyard
items.description: On Waiheke's northern tip, a rose-garden estate with sweeping Hauraki Gulf views to the Auckland skyline, a celebrated restaurant and cottages for those who want to stay the night. The most photographed cellar door on the island and a favourite for a special-occasion lunch.

items.name: Man O' War Vineyards
items.description: At the wild eastern end of Waiheke, a beachfront tasting room reached by a scenic drive through the island's largest private estate, pouring single-vineyard wines feet from the sand. Remote and unhurried; charter a boat or helicopter in for the most discreet arrival.

items.name: Rangitoto Island Summit Track
items.description: The perfect volcanic cone that frames every Auckland postcard, a 600-year-old island reached by a 25-minute ferry, climbed in about an hour through the world's largest pōhutukawa forest and black lava fields to a 259-metre crater rim. The summit view over the gulf and city is superb; bring a torch for the lava caves and sun protection for the exposed scoria.

items.name: Tiritiri Matangi Island Open Sanctuary
items.description: One of the world's great conservation successes, a predator-free island where you walk among some of New Zealand's rarest birds in the wild, takahē, kōkako, saddleback and stitchbird, that exist almost nowhere else so freely. A guided day with an island volunteer is a quiet privilege for nature-lovers; the ferry runs only Wednesday to Sunday, so book ahead.

items.name: Devonport & Mount Victoria
items.description: A 12-minute ferry to a genteel Victorian seaside village of bookshops, cafés and colonial villas, with the little cone of Mount Victoria offering a postcard view straight back to the city skyline. An effortless, charming half-day that even the least mobile of the party can enjoy from the waterfront.

items.name: North Head (Maungauika)
items.description: A headland cone above Devonport honeycombed with Victorian coastal-defence tunnels and gun emplacements, guarding the harbour entrance with commanding views over the gulf. A gentle walk-up with just enough history and dark passages to intrigue children.

items.name: Waitākere Ranges Regional Park
items.description: Sixteen thousand hectares of native rainforest, kauri stands and waterfalls dropping to the wild west coast, half an hour from the city. Note that a kauri-dieback protection programme has closed many forest tracks, go with a guide who knows what is open, and always use the boot-cleaning stations to protect the ancient trees.

items.name: Piha Beach
items.description: The most famous of Auckland's black-sand surf beaches, a dramatic ironsand crescent guarded by the great hulk of Lion Rock and pounded by Tasman swell. Wild, cinematic and beautiful, but the rips are serious, so swim only between the summer patrol flags and consider it a place to watch the surf rather than brave it.

items.name: Karekare Beach
items.description: The most secluded of the west-coast beaches, reached through rainforest and a stream crossing, its vast empty ironsand made famous as the setting of the Oscar-winning film The Piano. Utterly atmospheric and almost always deserted; there are no facilities, so come prepared.

items.name: Muriwai Beach & the Gannet Colony
items.description: A rugged black-sand coast where, from August to March, some 1,200 Australasian gannets nest on the clifftop at Ōtakamiro Point within metres of easy viewing platforms, an extraordinary wildlife spectacle with no effort required. Pair it with lunch at the nearby winery for a full west-coast morning.

items.name: Hunua Falls
items.description: A 30-metre waterfall spilling into a bush-fringed pool in the Hūnua Ranges, under an hour southeast of the city and far quieter than the western beaches. A short, easy path and a picnic make it a gentle escape into native forest; check current track status before you go.

items.name: Matakana Village & Wine Country
items.description: An hour north, a village of boutique galleries, a beloved Saturday farmers' market and a cluster of small wineries such as Brick Bay, whose sculpture trail winds through native bush and ponds. A civilised, low-key alternative to Waiheke for a day among vines, art and artisan food.

items.name: Tāwharanui Regional Park
items.description: An open sanctuary on a peninsula north of the city, ringing white-sand Anchor Bay with predator-proof fencing so that takahē roam the grassland and kiwi call at night. Among the finest beaches in the Auckland region and blissfully uncrowded on a weekday.

items.name: Goat Island Marine Reserve
credentials: New Zealand's first marine reserve (est. 1975)
items.description: New Zealand's first no-take marine reserve, established in 1975 near Leigh, where snapper, crayfish and rays crowd the shallows for snorkellers and a glass-bottomed boat. A rewarding half-day for families who want to see the sea life without diving; go on a calm, offshore-wind day for clear water.

items.name: Te Hana Te Ao Marama Cultural Centre
items.description: An hour north, Auckland's leading Māori cultural centre, where a traditional welcome, a guided walk through a replica fortified pā, a kapa haka performance and a hāngī earth-oven feast give a genuine, unhurried immersion. Arranged as a private group visit it is a dignified highlight for multi-generational travellers.

items.name: Waka Voyaging Experience
items.description: Paddle a waka hourua, a Māori ocean-going canoe, on the Waitematā with the Te Toki Voyaging Trust, learning traditional star-and-swell navigation from the descendants of the Pacific's greatest wayfinders. A rare, hands-on cultural encounter on the water rather than a staged show.

items.name: Waitomo Glowworm Caves (day trip)
items.description: About 2.5 hours south, a limestone cavern where you glide by boat beneath a ceiling of thousands of glowworms glimmering like a private galaxy, one of New Zealand's singular natural wonders. Best done as a private full-day drive, often combined with Hobbiton; the black-water rafting option is for the adventurous.

items.name: Hobbiton Movie Set, Matamata (day trip)
items.description: Two hours south, the immaculately kept Shire from the Lord of the Rings and Hobbit films, forty-four hobbit holes set in green Waikato farmland, ending with a drink at the Green Dragon Inn. A joyful, easy day for film-lovers and children; a private car and guide beats the coach tours for pace.

items.name: Coromandel Peninsula & Cathedral Cove (day trip)
items.description: About two hours east, a coast of pōhutukawa-fringed coves crowned by the great natural rock arch of Cathedral Cove and the geothermal quirk of Hot Water Beach, where you dig your own warm spa in the sand. A long but rewarding day; helicopter transfer turns it into an effortless outing and avoids the winding roads.

items.name: Rotorua Geothermal & Māori Culture (long day trip)
items.description: Around three hours south, the heart of Māori tourism and geothermal drama, bubbling mud, geysers, thermal spas and the living village of Whakarewarewa. It is a stretch as a single day, so most travellers stay a night; a helicopter or charter flight makes a day visit civilised.

items.name: Bay of Islands (overnight-worthy trip)
items.description: Roughly three hours north, a sub-tropical seascape of 144 islands, dolphin cruises, big-game fishing and the founding site of the nation at Waitangi. Truly it deserves an overnight, but a scenic flight or helicopter from Auckland can deliver a memorable single day of sailing and history.

items.name: Scenic Helicopter Flight over the Hauraki Gulf
items.description: Lift off from the waterfront or Ardmore for a private flight over the skyline, Rangitoto's crater and the vineyards of Waiheke, landing for a cellar-door lunch or a remote beach. The most discreet and time-efficient way for a family to see the City of Sails and reach the gulf islands in style.

items.name: Auckland Fish Market & Wynyard dining
items.description: A working fish market turned food destination on the waterfront, with oyster bars, a sushi counter and cooking classes celebrating the day's catch from the Hauraki Gulf. A lively, casual counterpoint to the fine-dining rooms and a good place to understand New Zealand seafood.

items.name: Paris Butter
items.description: One of Auckland's most refined tables, French technique applied to the best New Zealand produce across an ever-changing tasting menu in an elegant Herne Bay villa. The kind of hushed, special-occasion dinner discerning travellers seek; advise the kitchen of any vegetarian or Jain needs when booking.

items.name: Sidart
items.description: Chef Sid Sahrawat's flagship degustation room above Ponsonby, a long-running standard-bearer for creative fine dining in the city with polished wine pairings and warm service. Sahrawat's Indian heritage runs through his kitchens, so it is a considered choice for Indian palates seeking a tasting-menu evening.

items.name: Cassia
items.description: Sid Sahrawat's celebrated modern Indian restaurant, refined, contemporary cooking rooted in the subcontinent that has long topped Auckland's lists, a rare fine-dining Indian table of genuine ambition. Confirm the current location when booking, as the restaurant has relocated from its long-time SkyCity home.

items.name: Auckland Zoo
items.description: A well-regarded conservation zoo beside Western Springs park, with a night-time kiwi house where families can finally see New Zealand's shy national bird, plus native tuatara and a strong Australasian collection. An easy, shaded day for younger children.

items.name: Albert Park & the University Quarter
items.description: A formal Victorian park of fountains, statues and flowerbeds set between the Art Gallery and the university, a green pause in the heart of the city. A pretty, unhurried stroll to link a museum morning with lunch on High Street.

items.name: Motuihe & Motutapu Islands
items.description: Quieter neighbours to Rangitoto and Waiheke, predator-free islands of white-sand bays and gentle walking tracks that see a fraction of the crowds. Ideal for a private boat picnic day when you want the gulf to yourselves.

items.name: Ahi
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, Three Hats
items.description: Chef Ben Bayly's celebration of New Zealand producers, a refined, land-and-sea tasting menu that sits at the very top of the national game.

items.name: Cocoro
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, Three Hats
items.description: Chef Makoto Tokuyama's serene Japanese degustation, precise, seasonal and deeply personal, a perennial three-hat kitchen.

items.name: Paris Butter
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, Three Hats
items.description: French technique met with native New Zealand produce in a handsome villa, one of the most assured kitchens in the country.

items.name: Tala
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, Three Hats
items.description: A modern Pacific and Middle-Eastern-inflected tasting menu that vaulted to the top tier, bold, generous and unmistakably its own.

items.name: Sidart
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards, Three Hats (long-standing)
items.description: Sid Sahrawat's long-running degustation temple, inventive, technically dazzling cooking that has anchored the city's fine-dining scene for years.

items.name: Kazuya
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, Two Hats
items.description: A unique fine-dining fusion marrying French technique with Japanese precision, intimate, exacting and quietly one of the city's best.

items.name: Metita
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, Hotel Restaurant of the Year
items.description: Chef Michael Meredith's Pacific dining room in The Grand by SkyCity, the country's Hotel Restaurant of the Year, celebrating island flavours with polish.

items.name: Farina
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, Greenstone Creek Metropolitan Restaurant of the Year
items.description: Chef-owner Sergio Maglione's love letter to seafood, handmade pasta and Neapolitan pizza, Auckland's Metropolitan Restaurant of the Year.

items.name: Culprit
credentials: Viva Top 50 Restaurants, Auckland 2025, Supreme Winner
Cuisine Good Food Guide 2025, Hatted
items.description: Kyle Street and Jordan MacDonald's inventive, produce-driven room, the supreme winner of the Viva Top 50, doing something entirely its own.

items.name: Onslow
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, Two Hats
items.description: Josh Emett's elegant all-day dining room in a heritage building, refined, seasonal cooking with impeccable service.

items.name: Forest
credentials: Metro Restaurant of the Year 2025
Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, Innovation Award (Plabita Florence)
items.description: A tiny 17-seat room open just four evenings a week, Plabita Florence's intimate, personal cooking, named Metro's Restaurant of the Year.

items.name: Amano
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Guide 2025, recognised (Savor Group flagship)
A landmark Britomart dining room
items.description: A vast, buzzing Italian brasserie and bakery in Britomart, house-made pasta, wood-fired cooking and all-day energy.

items.name: Kingi
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Guide 2025, Hatted
A landmark Britomart seafood dining room
items.description: A sustainability-minded seafood room inside The Hotel Britomart, line-caught fish and shellfish, cooked simply and beautifully.

items.name: Cazador
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Guide 2025, Hatted
A Mount Eden institution
items.description: A long-loved family-run room celebrating wild game and nose-to-tail cooking, characterful, honest and quietly excellent.

items.name: Tempero
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, Specialist Restaurant of the Year
items.description: A vibrant Brazilian-rooted room celebrating live-fire and bold flavour, the country's Specialist Restaurant of the Year.

items.name: Apéro
credentials: Lewisham Awards 2025, Best Wine List & Best Chef
Cuisine Good Food Guide 2025, recognised
items.description: A cult natural-wine bar and bistro on K' Road, small, seasonal plates and one of the city's finest cellars.

items.name: Caretaker
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars, 50 Best Discovery listed
A landmark Auckland cocktail bar (est. 2015)
items.description: A New York-inspired basement speakeasy beneath Britomart, no menu, just a host who reads you and pours the perfect drink, with live jazz early in the week.

items.name: Deadshot
credentials: From the Caretaker stable, a benchmark Auckland cocktail lineage
A landmark Britomart cocktail bar
items.description: Caretaker's cooler, moodier sibling, effortlessly stylish, seated-only and welcoming, where you are led in once a table is free.

items.name: Panacea
credentials: Lewisham Awards 2025, Best Cocktail Experience
Lewisham Awards 2025, Best Sustainability
items.description: An inner-city cocktail kitchen and whisky bar with a sustainability ethos, inventive drinks and a serious spirits collection.

items.name: Annabel's
credentials: A landmark Ponsonby Road bar
Editorially recognised, Urban List / Denizen Auckland
items.description: A relaxed, characterful Ponsonby bar with a chilled vibe, live music, wine launches and guest-chef pop-ups in a much-loved neighbourhood room.

items.name: The Rooftop at QT
credentials: Atop QT Auckland, a landmark Viaduct rooftop bar
items.description: A glamorous rooftop terrace over the Viaduct marina, cocktails, colour and one of the best harbour views in the city.

plan.heading: 3 days in Auckland, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Check into the Hotel Britomart in the waterfront quarter, then the Auckland Art Gallery Toi o Tāmaki.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Wynyard and Viaduct harbours, and the volcanic cone of Maungawhau / Mount Eden for the view.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Ahi or Cocoro in Britomart, the city's most considered kitchens.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The ferry to Waiheke Island and a morning among the vineyards.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A cellar lunch at Mudbrick or Man O' War overlooking the Hauraki Gulf.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return on the evening ferry for a quiet dinner at Amano.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive west to the Waitākere Ranges and the black sand of Piha or Karekare.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Back through the bush, then the Maritime Museum and the harbour edge.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at Paris Butter or Sidart before departure.

items.name: Viaduct Harbour & Wynyard Quarter
items.description: Waterfront dining and marinas at the centre of the action; suits those who want the harbour on their doorstep.

items.name: Ponsonby
items.description: Villa-lined, café-heavy and stylish just west of the centre; for travellers who prefer neighbourhood restaurants to the tourist strip.

items.name: Waiheke Island
items.description: A 40-minute ferry to vineyards and beaches; suits a slower base that treats the city as an occasional day trip.

events.name: Auckland Anniversary Regatta
events.note: One of the world's largest one-day sailing regattas fills the harbour, the clearest expression of the City of Sails.

events.name: Pasifika Festival
events.note: The largest Pacific-culture festival in the world, with village stages, food and performance at Western Springs.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Indian passport holders need an NZeTA plus a visitor visa arranged before travel; make Waiheke Island a day or overnight for its wineries, and use Auckland as the gateway to a wider New Zealand itinerary rather than a destination in itself.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Land at Auckland International (AKL), a 30 to 45-minute chauffeured transfer into the city or to the waterfront; a helicopter can lift you straight to a Waiheke Island vineyard.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car suits the city and its edges, walking works around the Viaduct and Wynyard Quarter, and a short ferry carries you to Waiheke's vineyards and beaches.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM (One NZ, Spark or 2degrees) gives reliable 4G/5G in and around the city; wifi is standard in hotels.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Currency is the New Zealand dollar; cards and contactless are accepted everywhere and cash is rarely needed; tipping is not expected.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Summer Dec-Mar is warm, long-lit and best for the harbour and islands; winter Jun-Aug is mild but wet and windy, and shoulder months Nov and Apr are pleasant and quieter.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No reliable nonstop from India (a direct route is planned but not yet flying); the best one-stop is Singapore Airlines / Air New Zealand via Singapore, ~14h SIN-AKL plus the India-Singapore leg, roughly 20-22h total. Fly Singapore Airlines business to Changi, then Air New Zealand's Business Premier; both partners expanded India-NZ capacity for the 2026-27 season, so connections are good.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations; strict biosecurity as in Australia, declare all food, and note NZ can bar undeclared items. Tap water is safe and healthcare is excellent. Auckland is very safe. No altitude concern.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Strong for vegetarians and Jain travellers; a sizeable Indian community means authentic Indian food and pure-veg options across the city, and mainstream restaurants handle vegetarian well. Sandringham is Auckland's Indian food street and worth a dedicated visit.
